The Last Orbits of Man · Book One

The Last Orbits of Man: Descent

Out 15 December 2026 · Kindle & paperback

Earth has been silent for twenty-four years. Now someone is calling for help.

Read the full blurb

Earth has been silent for twenty-four years. Now someone is calling for help.

When the Bakali invaded, humanity lost its fleets, its cities and its home. Then the aliens released a pathogen that transformed billions of people into creatures still roaming the ruins.

The survivors fled to four distant space stations. Hidden across the solar system, they live aboard ageing machinery, protected by the few warships that escaped the invasion. Every patrol risks discovery. Every year, the Bakali return.

A transmission from beneath the Swiss Alps reveals that a group of scientists and marines has survived inside the Lazarus Facility. Their power is failing, their supplies are dwindling, and they cannot reach the surface alone. But they possess something that could give humanity a way to fight back.

For the crew of UES Prometheus, the last surviving Titan-class command carrier, the message means preparing for a mission few expected to make: a return to Earth.

Reaching the facility will mean crossing enemy-controlled space and sending troops into a world abandoned to the transformed. Committing ships to the rescue will leave the stations vulnerable—and the Bakali must never learn where humanity has been hiding.

The people inside Lazarus have waited twenty-four years for an answer. Humanity’s remaining fleet may have only one chance to reach them.

About the author

Big ideas. Human stories.

Hi, I’m Joseph R Holdsworth, also known as J.R.H., an independent science-fiction author from Wales and the creator of the Continuity series.

I’ve been fascinated by science fiction for as long as I can remember. Whether it’s humanity’s survival, first contact, distant worlds or the mysteries of the universe, I’ve always been drawn to big ideas that make you wonder, “What if?”

I don’t claim to be a seasoned professional. I’m learning with every book I write, but I’ve always had an imagination full of stories and scenarios I wanted to explore. Seeing ideas that once existed only in my head become real novels still feels surreal, and I’m proud to share them with you.

One of my biggest inspirations is A.G. Riddle, whose novels encouraged me to finally begin writing stories of my own. I’m also a huge admirer of Isaac Asimov, whose work helped shape my love of classic science fiction and ambitious world-building, and Stephen Baxter, whose scientifically grounded stories have inspired my fascination with humanity’s place in the universe.

Outside writing, I’m an enthusiastic Pokémon card collector. Like science fiction, it’s a hobby that has stayed with me over the years and continues to bring me a great deal of enjoyment.

Writing my first novel was something I once believed was beyond my reach. I was born with four learning disabilities, and for many years I lacked the confidence to pursue my dream of becoming an author. Eventually, I decided the only way to know what was possible was to try.

None of this would have been possible without the love and support of my wonderful fiancée, my amazing stepson and especially my beautiful daughter. At three days old, she suffered a neonatal stroke and now lives with epilepsy and cerebral palsy. Her strength, determination and courage inspire me every day.

“Limitations are the ones you set yourself.”

That journey led to the publication of my debut novel, Continuity: A Road to the Rift. The complete Continuity trilogy and The Last Fleet: When the Flags Fell are now available, along with The Rubin Anomaly: The Distortion and its sequel, Enveloped.

There are more stories in development, and I’m excited to keep sharing them. Thank you for visiting and supporting my work. I hope you’ll give my novels a go, and please do get in touch—I’d love to hear what you think.

The ideas behind the books

Inspiration behind the stories.

Some began with a documentary, others with a game or a question I couldn’t stop thinking about. Here’s how those ideas grew into my novels.

A question about survival

The Continuity series

Documentaries such as Evacuate Earth and How the Universe Works got me thinking about how humanity might survive a disaster on a planetary scale. One question stayed with me: what would happen if a black hole passed through our solar system, and how would ordinary people cope?

I began imagining the story almost like a film in my head: a changing world, families trying to reach safety, and the decisions humanity would have to make to survive. Those ideas became Continuity. Seeing that imagined world become a complete trilogy is something I’m very proud of.

Explore the trilogy →

Beyond the familiar universe

The Rubin Anomaly series

Watching The Twilight Zone and the 1990s series Sliders fed my fascination with strange realities and worlds beyond our own. Ideas about multiple universes added to that curiosity: what might exist beyond the universe we know?

I wanted to explore that sense of wonder and unease through a story of my own. The Rubin Anomaly grew from those questions, and from imagining how people might react when the familiar rules of their world begin to change.

Explore The Rubin Anomaly →

What about the Navy?

The Last Fleet: When the Flags Fell

This is my personal favourite of my novels. Playing the original Resident Evil on the PlayStation, watching Night of the Living Dead, and later enjoying World War Z and The Walking Dead all helped spark the idea.

I kept coming back to one question: what about the Navy? If an outbreak overwhelmed the land, could warships at sea offer a chance of survival? I wanted to explore what happened to those crews, how they might help others, and whether staying offshore would really be enough. That question became The Last Fleet, and I wanted to share it to see whether other readers had wondered the same thing.
